segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: Thus says the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works, your toil and your endurance, and that you cannot bear evil people. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them to be liars.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have endurance, and you have borne up for my name’s sake, and have not grown weary.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you have abandoned the love you had at first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So remember from where you have fallen; turn back and do the works you did at first. If not, I am coming to you, and I will remove your lampstand from its place, unless you turn back.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But this you do have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Smyrna write: Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and came to life:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your affliction and your poverty—yet you are rich—and the slander of those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested, and you will have affliction for ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. The one who conquers will never be harmed by the second death.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Pergamum write: Thus says the one who has the sharp two-edged sword:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know where you live, where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny your faith in me even in the days of Antipas, my witness, my faithful one, who was killed among you, where Satan lives.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold fast to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way you too have some who hold fast to the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So turn back. If not, I am coming to you soon, and I will make war on them with the sword of my mouth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Thyatira write: Thus says the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like burnished bronze:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works, and your love and faith and service and endurance, and that your last works are greater than your first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet, and she teaches and leads my slaves astray, to commit sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I gave her time to turn back, and she is not willing to turn back from her sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I am throwing her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they turn back from her works;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and I will kill her children with plague. Then all the assemblies will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching, who have not come to know the deep things of Satan, as they call them, I say: I lay no other burden on you;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: only hold fast to what you have until I come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end—to that one I will give authority over the nations,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: to shepherd them with an iron rod, as clay vessels are shattered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: just as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give that one the morning star.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.

notes.note: Nearly all English translations use 'church', and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a city's citizen gathering and, from the Greek Scriptures, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses 'assembly' wherever the word occurs.

The Greek word means 'messenger', human or heavenly. Because it means a heavenly being everywhere else in Revelation, most scholars take it so here, as a heavenly counterpart or representative of each community. Others think it means a human messenger or leader. The 'you' addressed in each message is singular but plainly has the whole community in view.

Most translations keep 'repent', an established term that readers take to include a change of life. In current English, though, 'repent' centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, and here the command is in fact to go back to earlier practice.

Nothing certain is known about this group beyond what this chapter says. Verses 14–15 appear to associate their teaching with eating food offered to idols and sexual immorality. Later Christian writers connected them with the Nicolaus of Acts 6:5, but that link may be no more than a guess from the name.

This is the language of a dispute within the Jewish world of the first century. The writer is himself Jewish and treats 'Jew' as an honourable name, which he denies to a local group that was denouncing the believers in Smyrna. 'Synagogue' simply means 'gathering', and the phrase is probably a bitter inversion of the scriptural 'gathering of the Lord'. It is not a statement about the Jewish people as a whole, though it has often been misused that way.

Pergamum was a leading centre of Roman power and emperor worship in the province of Asia. It had a temple to Augustus and Rome, a monumental altar of Zeus and a famous shrine of the healing god Asclepius. Which of these the phrase refers to, or whether it means the city's pagan and imperial character as a whole, is disputed.

The Greek is literally 'my faith'. Most translations understand it as faith directed toward Jesus, as rendered here. It could also mean 'your faithfulness to me', which would fit the description of Antipas as 'my faithful one' in the same sentence.

The Greek is a broad term for sexual conduct outside what the law permits, and the older 'fornication' is now obsolete and narrower. The allusion is to Numbers 25 and 31:16, where Israelite men were drawn into sex with Moabite women and into worship of their gods. In the prophets the same word group is a common image for unfaithfulness to God. Scholars disagree whether here and in verses 20–21 it is meant literally, figuratively of taking part in pagan worship, or both.

The word means a pebble or small stone. Such stones were used for voting, including a white one for acquittal in a jury's verdict, and also as admission tokens and as amulets inscribed with names. Which custom lies behind the image is uncertain, and no explanation has won general agreement.

The Greek word meant a person owned by another, and its hearers knew that. Many translations use 'servants' or 'bondservants', partly to avoid associations with modern race-based slavery, while several recent ones use 'slaves'. The word here expresses belonging wholly to Christ as master.

Jezebel is almost certainly a symbolic name, not the woman's real one. It recalls the queen in 1 Kings who promoted the worship of Baal in Israel and opposed the prophet Elijah. Some manuscripts read 'your wife Jezebel', but this is generally judged a secondary reading.

The Greek says simply 'a bed'. To be thrown onto a bed was an idiom for being struck down with illness, and that sense fits the parallel with 'great affliction', so many modern translations render it 'sickbed' or 'bed of suffering'. There is probably also an ironic contrast with the bed of adultery.

The Greek is literally 'kill with death'. Many translations take this as an emphatic Semitic idiom, 'strike dead'. In the Greek Old Testament, however, 'death' regularly translates the Hebrew word for pestilence, and it has that sense in Revelation 6:8, so 'plague' is the more likely meaning here. 'Her children' probably means her followers.

The Greek is literally 'kidneys and hearts', echoing Jeremiah 17:10 and similar passages. In biblical idiom the kidneys are the seat of a person's most hidden feelings and motives. English has no equivalent use of the word, so the phrase is rendered by its meaning.

These words come from Psalm 2:9 in its ancient Greek version. The Hebrew there reads 'break', but the Greek translators read the same consonants as 'shepherd'. The verb is the ordinary one for tending a flock and was a common figure for governing, so most translations have 'rule'. This translation keeps the image the Greek reader met, although the iron rod and shattered pottery show that the shepherding here is severe.

candidates.reason: Recurs across Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation, and translations vary between 'patience', 'perseverance', 'steadfastness' and 'endurance'.
A key verb in Revelation and the Johannine writings; 'overcome', 'conquer' and 'be victorious' are all in use, and variation would hide a deliberate refrain.
Frequent throughout the New Testament; 'tribulation', 'affliction', 'distress', 'suffering' and 'persecution' all compete, and 'great tribulation' has become a technical term that may mislead.
Occurs in the Gospels, Paul, 1 Peter and Revelation with the related verb σκανδαλίζω; renderings range over 'stumbling block', 'trap', 'offence' and 'cause of sin'.

Used of Christ, church leaders and the Psalm 2 iron-rod passages (Matthew 2:6; John 21:16; Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2; Revelation 7:17, 12:5, 19:15); a decision is needed between 'shepherd', 'rule' and 'tend'.
